meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'This is no time to be making new enemies'?
meta.ogDescription: A deathbed joke, not a Machiavelli line. Earliest print: a Newgate convict, Staffordshire Advertiser, 13 June 1795. Machiavelli was credited only in 1981.

answer.label: Not Machiavelli — an anonymous joke from 1795
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator traces this deathbed gag to an unnamed condemned prisoner at Newgate in the Staffordshire Advertiser of 13 June 1795, and concludes the anecdote is probably fictional. It was fastened onto Machiavelli only in 1981, over four centuries after his death, and appears nowhere in his own writings.

source.heading: The 1795 original — no philosopher in sight

source.excerpt: One of the criminals lately under sentence of death in Newgate, was visited by the Ordinary, who gravely urged him to acknowledge the justice of his sentence, &c. to which the culprit answering—the Divine demanded to know whether he renounced the D—l and all his works?—to which the poor fellow shrugging his shoulders, replied—that he begged to be excused, for, as he was going to a strange country, he did not wish to make himself any enemies.
trail: The oldest telling has no famous name in it at all. The Staffordshire Advertiser of 13 June 1795 tells it of an anonymous prisoner under sentence of death in Newgate who, asked whether he renounced the devil, “begged to be excused, for, as he was going to a strange country, he did not wish to make himself any enemies” (Quote Investigator ↗).

Through the nineteenth century the speaker is a stock character rather than a person. The Springfield Republican of 30 April 1856 gives it to a dying Irishman called Pat — “I’m going into a strange country, and I don’t want to make myself enemies!” — and by 1900 the Washington News Letter has reassigned it to a Scotsman (Quote Investigator ↗). Stephen Goranson had mapped the same 1856 Irishman versions for the American Dialect Society list in February 2012 (ADS-L ↗).

A named person finally attaches in 1952, and it is not a philosopher: Harry Hershfield’s New York Times column has the wit Wilson Mizner say it about a dying friend, not on his own deathbed. Voltaire only inherits the line by 1974, in a column in The Gleaner of Kingston, Jamaica (Quote Investigator ↗).

Machiavelli is last in the queue. The earliest version Quote Investigator finds is a 1981 paper by the economist Robert Lekachman, in which a cardinal at the bedside gets the answer “Now is not the time to make new enemies” — Lekachman introduces it as a story he recalls, not as a document. A 1990 Manila Standard column repeats it with the same hedges (“It is said that… Machiavelli is said to have replied”), and Quote Investigator’s verdict on the whole family is that it is “probably fictional” (Quote Investigator ↗).
source.excerptNote: The oldest version Quote Investigator can find. Note what is missing: no Machiavelli, no Voltaire, no cardinal — and not yet the snappy modern wording. The punchline is a shrug from a nameless convict.

source.rightsNote: The 1795 newspaper anecdote is long out of copyright, but it does not contain the modern sentence. The wording people actually circulate has no identified author at all, and the printings closest to it sit in twentieth-century, still-copyrighted sources — a 1952 New York Times column, a 1974 Gleaner piece, Robert Lekachman’s 1981 conference paper — so we assert no rights status for it.

author.heading: Who Machiavelli actually was
author.metaLine: 3 May 1469 – 21 June 1527 · Florentine diplomat and political theorist
author.bio: Machiavelli was appointed Second Chancellor of the Republic of Florence in 1498 and spent his working life as a diplomat and administrator, not as a court intriguer. The Prince, the book that turned his surname into an adjective, was written in 1513 and published only in 1532 — after his death — as were the Discourses in 1531. Five centuries of reputation as literature’s great cynic have made him one of the internet’s most reliable magnets for clever lines he never wrote.

copyAttribution: Not Machiavelli. This deathbed joke first appears in print on 13 June 1795 in the Staffordshire Advertiser, told of an anonymous prisoner under sentence of death at Newgate who, asked whether he renounced the devil, "begged to be excused, for, as he was going to a strange country, he did not wish to make himself any enemies." It was told of an Irishman by 1856 and a Scotsman by 1900, attached to Wilson Mizner in 1952, to Voltaire by 1974, and to Machiavelli only in 1981. Quote Investigator judges the anecdote probably fictional. — Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: A joke with a revolving cast
misattribution.intro: This is not one misattribution but a chain of them. The anecdote is a portable joke that has been re-cast roughly every generation, each time onto whoever seemed the most deliciously unrepentant figure available. Quote Investigator lays out the sequence.

items.scope: The version you have probably seen
items.why: The earliest Machiavelli telling Quote Investigator locates is a 1981 paper by the economist Robert Lekachman, where a cardinal at the bedside is answered “Now is not the time to make new enemies.” Lekachman offers it as a story he recalls, and a 1990 Manila Standard column repeats it as something Machiavelli “is said to have replied” (Quote Investigator ↗). Wikiquote’s Machiavelli page does not carry the line in any section (Wikiquote ↗).

The Voltaire telling is only seven years older than the Machiavelli one. Quote Investigator’s earliest instance is a 1974 column in The Gleaner of Kingston, Jamaica: “I don’t think at this time of life I should start making enemies” (Quote Investigator ↗).

items.scope: The first named human being in the chain
items.why: Harry Hershfield’s New York Times column of 21 September 1952 has Mizner deliver the line at someone else’s bedside — “This is no time for him to antagonize anybody” — so even here the dying man is not the wit (Quote Investigator ↗).

items.who: A dying Irishman, then a Scotsman
items.why: Before any celebrity was involved the speaker was an ethnic stock character: “Pat” in the Springfield Republican of 30 April 1856, a Scotsman in the Washington News Letter by 1900 (Quote Investigator ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: Nobody famous said it. The oldest version on record, from 1795, is told of a man whose name the newspaper did not bother to print — and Quote Investigator’s conclusion is that the anecdote is “probably fictional” in every version, including that one (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: Why it stuck to him
lead: A joke needs a plausible mouth to come out of, and Machiavelli’s is close to perfect. His name has been shorthand for cheerful amorality for five centuries, so a story in which he declines, with his last breath, to burn a bridge with the devil does not need evidence to feel true. That is exactly the mechanism to distrust: the more characteristic a quotation sounds, the less anyone checks it.

The chronology gives the game away. The line was already two centuries old and had been told about a Newgate convict, an Irishman and a Scotsman before any famous person got near it — and when the celebrities finally arrived, Voltaire in the 1970s and Machiavelli in the 1980s, they arrived last, in retellings that hedge with “it is said” and “I recall the story.”
context.detailsSummary: There is a real Machiavelli deathbed story — and it is also disputed
detailsBody: Machiavelli does have a celebrated deathbed legend, but it is a different one. In it he describes a vision of two crowds: the ragged poor of paradise, and a company of the damned that includes Plato, Aristotle, Seneca, Plutarch and Tacitus. Asked which he would rather join, he says he would much rather be in Hell with those great geniuses, talking politics, than shut up with the other lot.

Wikiquote files that story under Disputed too. It was first published by Étienne Binet in Du salut d’Origène in 1629, a century after Machiavelli died, with an earlier and more oblique reference to his “famous dream” in a letter of Giovanni Battista Busini in 1549 (Wikiquote ↗). Deathbeds are where quotations go to be invented.
context.pull: The joke is older than the attribution by nearly two centuries — and it was funny when nobody was attached to it at all.
